With the rising stock market also generating some wealth effects, sentiment among high-income households is likely to hold up. That said, rising prices continue to be a headwind for low- and middle-income households, and personal consumption increasingly seems to be getting polarized in Japan. Supply-side constraints: Business investment recorded an increase of just 0.2% q/q in Q4 following a 0.3 % contraction in Q3. The Bank of Japan’s December Tankan survey indicated that the corporates’ capex appetite remains strong. Still, the high-investment plans partly highlight the higher construction costs and capital-goods prices caused by the JPY’s depreciation and rising labour costs. Overall, the muted real GDP growth reflects, in no small part, a low potential growth rate and the economy already close to full employment, in our view. On a nominal basis, GDP grew by a solid 0.6 % q/q (2.3 % q/q), and the GDP deflator remained strong at 3.4 % y/y in Q4 (versus 3.5 % in Q3). records.text: ief, demographic headwinds in many European economies are likely to overwhelm any technological tailwinds, resulting in lower growth compared to the 2000-2024 period. Germany, Italy, Spain, China, South Korea, and the Euro area as a whole are particularly vulnerable, with aging dynamics poised to outweigh benefits from AI adoption. Against this backdrop, certain sectors look positioned to cap- ture sustained demand driven by demographic shifts. The Healthcare sector - spanning Pharmaceuticals, Biotechnol- ogy, and Medical devices - is a clear beneficiary, with the ris- ing prevalence of chronic conditions fueling demand. Medical device manufacturers producing cardiovascular equipment, pacemakers, hearing aids, and orthopedic implants are experi- encing robust growth, alongside expanding markets for health technology and remote monitoring wearables. Senior care services-encompassing assisted living facilities, nursing homes, independent living communities, and home- based care, are seeing heightened demand as preferences shift toward aging in place. Wealth management, retirement plan- ning, and Life and Health Insurance are also set to expand as financial services firms navigate the complexities of man- aging assets and care costs for an older client base. We also see potential for rising expenditure on leisure, travel, beauty, and anti-aging products tailored to older consumers, while Pharmaceutical retail benefits from sustained prescription medication demand among seniors.

Therefore, it is natural to think that the political hurdle for the opposition in the Upper House to reject a nomination is higher than it was in the past. n Profile of potential successors: Following convention, the successor to Member Noguchi, who comes from academia, is likely to be chosen from a similar background, such as a university professor. Meanwhile, the successor to Member Nakagawa would typically be expected to be a woman from the financial industry. However, with Ms. Koeda already on the board, the "female slot" is considered filled. Furthermore, with three members currently from the financial industry, it is quite possible that, for the sake of balance, a candidate could be chosen from outside the financial sector (for example, from industry or academia). If the nomination for Ms. Nakagawa's successor is presented at the same time, this choice has the potential to be the bigger surprise. Furthermore, considering that the opposition parties currently tend to favor more aggressive fiscal and monetary policies, it is relatively more likely that the nominee will be a "dove" rather than a "hawk." records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 317/02/2026 Moves to formalise a fiscal anchor: The NT has contextualised the current policy environment as being at a “significant fiscal inflection point”, (Business Day). This is not primarily as a result of the current more favourable cyclical revenue backdrop, but rather the NT’s recommitment to restraint of non-interest spending and a clearer, more transparent and “principles-led” approach to debt and deficit consolidation. This is reflected to a large degree in our own estimates (Figures 5 and 6). In May 2025 the NT released a fiscal anchors discussion document. The idea was to float different ideas about feasible implementation of a formal fiscal anchor or rule. This is something which policymakers in South Africa have long debated, but which has garnered more momentum in the past five years under the Ramaphosa administration (and now the GNU). A hard numerical rule remains off the table: The NT has been clear that it wants to avoid a dogmatic numerical rule (binding limits on debt levels or deficits). It is aiming for political flexibility to respond to different unforeseen shocks, particularly given the country’s still challenging socio-economic climate and grave infrastructure constraints which are beginning to build – Johannesburg’s worsening water infrastructure crisis is a good example. Within core inflation, lower shelter and household operations costs were offset by a GST/HST holiday-driven increase in alcoholic beverages, recreation, and health and personal care. Elevated headline CPI continues to reflect base effects from the temporary GST/HST holiday that ran from mid-December 2024 to mid-February 2025 and applied to roughly 10% of the CPI basket. The tax exemption generated pronounced monthly price declines in affected categories—including restaurant food, alcoholic beverages, toys, games and hobby supplies, children’s clothing, and selected grocery items such as snack foods and confectionery. As those artificially low prices drop out of the 12-month comparison window, they are mechanically lifting year-over-year inflation.For example, restaurant food prices were 12.3% higher in January 2026 compared with January 2025, when prices were temporarily depressed by the GST/HST break. These differences reflect the current level of maturity, as well as advantages and challenges unique to each segment. Autonomous vehicles sit at the more advanced end of the spectrum: development has been underway for nearly a decade, production closely aligns with existing automotive supply chains, and models can be trained on large volumes of real-world driving datasets collected from millions of conventional, human-driven cars already on the road. This data comes from advanced driver-assistance systems, onboard sensors and fleet telematics. Humanoid robots sit at the opposite end. Adoption will likely take longer, constrained by far more limited physical AI training data, the complexity of integrating models with hardware control systems, and ongoing battery-power limitations. 17 February 2026 3 Barclays | AI gets physical

records.text: gns—the narrowness of job growth and the continued decline in job openings—are more concerning. While the labor market remains shaky, we expect the recent stabilization to n persist for the rest of the year, with only a small uptick in the unemployment rate to 4.5% from here. The latest pickup in job growth is not entirely convincing just yet, but the strong final demand growth and less volatile policy environment that we expect this year should produce a small pick-up in hiring, and a small pick-up is all that should be needed to sustain job growth at the breakeven pace. We continue to see the risks to our labor market forecast as tilted toward a worse n outcome and see this as the key risk for 2026. One reason is that the starting point for labor demand is still concerning—job growth has been weak and narrow, job openings are still trending lower, and companies do not appear eager to hire. But the main reason is the risk of a faster and more disruptive deployment of artificial intelligence. For now, though, job losses from AI appear visible but moderate, the layoff scare from last fall looks somewhat less concerning, and hiring restraint at companies eyeing the possibilities of AI looks like a manageable headwind. records.text: Europe’s M&A trails the US amid fewer tech and mega-deals Comparing the sector mix and deal sizes of European vs. US strategic M&A highlights important differences between the two markets. In 2025, Financials accounted for the largest share of European M&A volumes vs. about 9% in the US. By contrast, Computers and Electronics represented roughly 20% of US strategic M&A volumes vs. 9% in Europe (left panel, Exhibit 2). Deal size is another key differentiator. Transactions larger than $20 billion represented roughly 36% of US strategic M&A volumes last year, while Europe recorded none (right panel, Exhibit 2). In fact, Europe last recorded a deal larger than $20 billion in 2022, and activity has since been skewed toward the $1 billion to $10 billion range. Taken together, the sector and size mix suggests the bar remains high for any near-term convergence in strategic M&A volumes vs. the US. These differences are largely structural, reflecting the US market’s larger Tech footprint and greater presence of mega cap firms. records.text: Appendix Methodology: Estimating the physical AI market We base our current and projected market-size estimates on a broad set of public sources available through AlphaSense, including company reports, earnings calls, research publications and investor presentations. We begin by gathering a diverse set of reports that offer both current estimates and forward-looking projections for each of the four physical AI market segments (humanoid robots, autonomous vehicles, drones and industrial robots). In total, our sample includes over 30 reports published in 2024 and 2025. Arriving at a precise figure is difficult because published estimates vary widely in definitions and scope. We address this by relying on sources that use broad definitions. For drones, our projections cover commercial, defence, delivery, inspection, logistics and agricultural units. For autonomous vehicles, we include levels 1 through 5 of autonomy. For humanoids, we focus on all bipedal robots. For industrial robots, our estimates also encompass logistics systems, AI- guided robotic arms, collaborative robots (cobots), autonomous mobile robots and warehouse robots for picking, sorting and transport. Our data sources draw on estimates from Grand View Research (covering drones and autonomous vehicles), the Business Research Company, PR Newswire, and a range of company reports from firms including Xer Tech, Kranti Group, TCI, and BYD Electronics. Mapping the global physical AI value chain Given the significant growth potential we identify, this report sets out to build the macro narrative for how physical AI could reshape economic dynamics across sectors and countries. As no comprehensive dataset of the companies behind the physical AI value chain currently exists, we construct our own – representing a key innovation of this work. We adopt a bottom-up approach to ground our macro analysis in the underlying industry structure. We begin by developing a conceptual framework that decomposes the physical AI value chain into its foundational blocks. We then analyse each block in turn, identifying close to 200 relevant public issuers that could potentially be involved in this theme over the next decade. From this universe, 100 are also credit issuers (ie, they have at least one active corporate bond outstanding), underscoring the relevance of this theme to both credit and equity investors. As of January 2026, the credit issuers in our sample have 2,300 active bonds totalling $1.5trn in amount outstanding, creating a sizeable footprint across major credit benchmarks. This universe represents 16% of the Bloomberg EM Asia USD Credit Index, 10% of the Bloomberg US Corporate Investment Grade Index and 6% of the Bloomberg Pan-European Corporate Index. Economics Europe Blog Date 17 February 2026 The China Price: Tracking disinflation risk through imports The December ECB Accounts referred to the ‘second China shock ’ as a major challenge for the euro area economy. There are two dimensions to consider. The first is the direct transmission of Chinese excess capacity and low inflation via imports into lower euro area inflation. The second is the indirect transmission via lower production as China increasingly competes with European goods on global markets. In this note we focus on the former. We find a tangible but limited drag on euro area inflation so far. • Consumer price impact: offsetting forces at play. We do a deep -dive into import prices from a selection of the euro area’s main trading partners and estimate a contribution to euro area consumer prices . At the local currency level (pre-FX adjustment), there is no "China drag" on prices. In fact, a positive contribution from partners like the US, Poland, and Czechia overwhelms China's near-zero impulse. German households on aggregate saved a gross 20% of their disposable income in 2024 (Figure 4). This is one of the highest savings rates in Europe and clearly above the EU average of 13.2%. But households keep a large share of their financial assets in bank deposits and insurance policies (Figure 5), which for a long time have yielded only modest interest income, hindering wealth accumulation. records.text: 16 February 2026 Focus Germany Page 18 Deutsche Bank AG 5) Conclusion The proposed reform of private pension provision, slated for implementation in early 2027, aims to create a more attractive, transparent, and return-oriented third pillar of retirement savings in Germany. A key novelty is the planned “old-age provision account” that would allow for investments where the investor is taking the risk and there are no guarantees (up to risk class 5, implying up to 100% equity exposure). This opens the door for effective low-cost solutions with possibly much higher returns than under the old Riester model which has serious drawbacks. The proposal includes several elements of other well-established private pension systems like ensuring a lifecycle investment approach and the offering of standard products. Still, the tax incentives (incl. public grants) seem modest, and the 1.5% cost cap relatively high when compared to other countries. Moreover, guarantee products with potentially significantly lower returns will still be available and may remain a popular choice. Perhaps the biggest issue, there continues to be an opt-in rather than an opt-out or even mandatory enrolment, which could result in an insufficient participation rate. Nevertheless, the reform is crucial given that the pay-as-you-go system faces mounting strain from an aging population, and supplementary private pension income therefore becomes absolutely vital. We see UK labour demand as likely flat to mildly negative at the start of the year, and as likely to remain flat over 1H26. Prints like this make us worried that we are too optimistic. The jobless rate at 5.2% is a post-pandemic high. It is likely to edge higher in the coming months, although we still struggle to see it breaching 5.5%, precisely because of our view of flat employment growth. Amid a sharp slowdown in inward migration, and given less of a pull to the labour market from inactivity due to a dearth of jobs, we would need to see further headcount reduction, we think, for the jobless rate to rise notably higher from here. This is still a risk - but one that might materialise in response to a further deterioration in growth. European M&A: Sentiment Improves, Debt-Funded Deal Boom Unlikely Strategic M&A volumes in Europe reached roughly $257 billion last year. That was near the upper end of the historical range and about 16% higher than the prior year. Still, European volumes were well below the roughly $1.4 trillion recorded in the US, up about 65% from 2024 and close to a record high. The gap is equally apparent in credit markets, which saw just €7 billion of M&A-related issuance in EUR IG last year vs. roughly $146 billion in USD IG (Exhibit 1). In this Global Markets Daily, we discuss why this divergence is likely to persist and what signals from recent firm transcripts imply for the European M&A pipeline. Overall, the evidence suggests the recent increase in European M&A is cyclical, but it lacks the broad-based optimism typically associated with a sustained step-up in debt-funded deals. As a result, we think near-term EUR IG M&A-related supply risk should remain modest relative to the USD market. Our analysis of the direct price dimension of the ‘second China shock' yields three key conclusions: 1) the 'pure' trade impulse at the local currency level is actually slightly inflationary, as China's near -zero contribution is overwhelmed by rising prices from other partners ; 2) the euro's appreciation against the renminbi is the dominant driver, single -handedly reversing this dynamic to create a net disinflationary impulse into consumer prices – albeit a small one (c.0.25pp); 3) the likelihood of a more dramatic future impulse depends critically on domestic Chinese factors: the sooner "anti -involution" policies put a floor under producer prices (and/or the RMB appreciates), the more contained the downward external price risk will be. These direct price dynamics need close monitoring to ensure they remain contained. The more profound and forward -looking concern, however, may be shifting from a direct price effect via imports to an indirect price effect via activity. While the immediate impact on headline consumer prices appears manageable, the underlying competitive pressure from China poses a structural challenge to the Euro Area economy. Should this competition lead to significant margin compression and corporate distress, it might not only dampen employment, investment and GDP but also erode Europe's industrial capacity in critical sectors. BLS computes seasonally adjusted data using seasonal factors derived by the X-13ARIMA- SEATS Seasonal Adjustment Method. These factors are updated with the release of January data in February and reflect price movements from the previous calendar year. This process typically requires that 60 consecutive recent observations for both CPI-U and CPI-W be available at a minimum. When a month of data for a directly adjusted series (CPI-U or CPI-W) is not available due to inadequacy for publication, BLS no longer seasonally adjusts either series until sufficient data is available again. Due to the 2025 lapse in funding, BLS could not publish October 2025 indexes for most CPI series. This resulted in BLS using atypical methods in order to maintain a continuous time series on which to calculate revised seasonal factors, including a seasonal factor for October 2025. For the seasonal adjustment process, BLS approximated the missing October data by taking the geometric mean of the September and November index values. The results confirm a story of countervailing forces. At the local currency level (i.e., before euro conversion), the data show a fading positive impulse from China on the one hand and a persistent positive impulse from other trading partners on the other. records.text: M Update 2 January CPI: Noisy Headline, Encouraging Core Bank of Canada Implications In our view, the Bank of Canada has reached the end of its easing cycle. In our forecasts, we expect that the next move will be hike, and we have currently penciled in 1Q27 for this move. The January inflation print did not show any surprises, and for now, there do not appear to be any demand-side pressures visible that could lead to upside inflation risks. The 3-month saar average of the CPI Trim and Median continues to move lower, and shelter has been running soft. Risks around our call are asymmetric. On the downside, further weakening in household and business demand would raise the likelihood of additional easing. January’s labor market data already point to cooling nominal wage growth; a sharper deceleration in real wages would weigh on consumption and push growth below the BoC’s forecast, particularly in 2H26. In that scenario, especially if CUSMA risks intensify, the BoC could move into fully accommodative territory, cutting rates below neutral. On the upside, we see limited scope for earlier tightening. We do not expect the BoC to hike before 4Q26, ahead of our 1Q27 baseline. Both we and the BoC assume a recovery in demand in 2H26, contingent on CUSMA remaining in place. With inflation expected to be moderate by year end, the earliest case for hikes would require clear evidence of growth stabilization. Mercedes-Benz uses Nvidia’s Omniverse to virtually retool factories with minimal disruption. Stellantis has rolled out cloud-based digital twins and 3D vision tools across its manufacturing network. Beyond manufacturing, digital twins increasingly support the full vehicle lifecycle. Looking ahead, the next phase is likely to move from plant-level twins toward fully integrated, end-to-end supply-chain ecosystems. records.text: os and components: factories first, vehicle content later Physical AI is likely to drive incremental demand for motion components, with actuators at the forefront. However, the near-term value in autos is less about per-vehicle content and more about factory automation and digital twins8 , where AI can deliver meaningful opex and capex savings. Incremental vehicle-level content emerges primarily where AI enables drive-by-wire, ADAS and software-defined subsystems, such as brake and steering actuators and active chassis systems. As robots such as humanoids and mobile robots move beyond pilot projects and start operating continuously in real-world environments, demand is rising for reliable motion components, especially actuators that can reliably perform physical tasks. In this context, incumbent mechatronics expertise from the 'analog age' becomes a real advantage as AI shifts from software into physical movement. At the same time, digital twins are becoming a standard tool across the automotive industry as vehicles become more digital and AI-enabled. Digital twins let companies design, test and optimise in a simulated environment before making changes in the real world. This helps reduce costs, speed up development, improve safety and minimise downtime. 17 February 2026 9 Barclays | AI gets physical

The current reform proposal aims for a more attractive, transparent, and return- oriented third pillar of retirement savings. It is slated for implementation in early 2027. The reform is crucial given that the first pillar, the public pay-as-you-go system, faces mounting strain from demographic change, and therefore supplementary private pension income becomes vital, as in other countries. The existing Riester model has serious drawbacks, including low returns and high costs. A key novelty is the planned “old-age provision account”. It would move away from expensive mandatory guarantee products and allow up to 100% equity exposure. This opens the door for effective low-cost solutions with possibly much higher returns. The proposal also includes elements of other countries’ successful pension systems. Still, the tax incentives (incl. public grants) seem modest, and the 1.5% cost cap relatively high. Moreover, guarantee products will remain available. Perhaps the biggest issue is people will still have to actively sign up for the scheme (“opt-in”), which could limit participation. records.text: EMerging Resilience 1. EMerging resilience EM assets, in particular equities and local rates, have enjoyed a strong start in 2026 after a year of stellar returns in 2025. Despite more challenging valuations, our view is that EM assets can still yield sturdy returns this year given a macro backdrop of solid growth, low inflation and non-recessionary Fed cuts. That said, given the strong recent run in EMs and corresponding pick-up in positioning, investors are increasingly concerned about the risk of EM drawdowns, especially with rising geopolitical tensions and higher volatility in core FX and equity markets. Shocks that lead to drawdowns can manifest from two broad sources: from within EMs themselves because underlying macro conditions deteriorate or political shifts precipitate volatility, or from the global cross-asset environment. While both are relevant, in this piece, we focus primarily on the shocks emanating from global market conditions. Such concern is warranted given the historical volatility of EM assets and underperformance around periods of heightened risk aversion and global uncertainty. However, as we demonstrate, EM assets have demonstrated a growing resilience to external market shocks in recent years. As a result, we are taking profit on the position, booking a 7.7bp (USD38.5k) profit. The local curve has steepened over the past few days as the Ministry of Finance surprised the market by selling Coltes 35s intensively to improve its cash position. Likewise, January’s CPI print coming in line with expectations put downward pressure on the 2y node, adding to the steepening bias on the local curve. We consider the belly of the curve highly attractive, reflecting our view of a potential swing in Colombia’s political pendulum in the run-up to May’s presidential election. We will monitor the opportune timing to re-express our view. To recap, we entered the trade on 13 January in anticipation of a move to the center-right/right in May’s election. records.text: European transcripts signal improving M&A sentiment To gauge the forward-looking pulse of European M&A, we screen earnings call transcripts for the 47 largest European non-financial firms and the 14 largest European financial firms in the EUR IG corporate credit index. After excluding non-European issuers, this universe represents about €1.1 trillion of debt outstanding, or roughly 50% of the EUR IG market. As shown in the left panel of Exhibit 3, the frequency of M&A-related language has tracked strategic M&A volumes reasonably well since 2016. Mentions have also trended higher across our sample, averaging roughly 650 references over the past year (as of Q4) vs. about 500 in 2024 Q1. The increase has been most pronounced among financial firms, consistent with their outsized contribution to European M&A last year. We then extend the screen beyond deal-specific language and classify transcript mentions into five macro themes: 1) Macroeconomic headwinds and tailwinds, 2) Government policy (including regulation and tax), 3) China and competitive strategy, 4) Innovation and digital transformation, and 5) Tariffs. records.text: Early Steps Toward Labor Market Stabilization The January employment report offered more evidence that the labor market is taking early steps toward the stabilization that we and the FOMC expect this year, though other recent data, in particular the recent decline in job openings, have been weaker, and the case for stabilization is still preliminary. The news has likely been good enough on net for the FOMC to judge that further rate cuts are not urgent. Because it will take a while for year-over-year inflation to come down enough to cut purely for the sake of normalization, even in our optimistic inflation forecast, the labor market would likely have to weaken again to trigger a rate cut much before our June forecast for the next cut (which we expect to be followed by a second 25bp cut in September). In this week’s Analyst, we review the latest evidence on labor supply, labor demand, the prospects for stabilization this year, and the downside risks presented by layoff news and artificial intelligence. Labor supply: How many jobs do we need to create each month? Labor supply growth has declined sharply as immigration has fallen from the peak reached in late 2023. We estimate that net immigration averaged 1mn in the 2010s and fell to 0.5mn on average in 2025 and 0.4mn annualized in recent months. It can also have positive knock-on effects on the economy as a whole. Pension assets, by definition, are long-term capital as they are locked in over a period of 30 years or more. Thus, they are well positioned to finance innovative, high-growth companies and infrastructure investments. In return, through their investment, future pensioners can benefit from the resulting economic growth. Europe urgently needs more long-term capital to close its investment gap and improve its competitiveness as laid out in the Draghi report . Underdeveloped funded pension pillars are a key reason behind underdeveloped equity (and venture capital) markets in many EU countries. An intra-EU comparison shows that economies with higher household claims on pension funds and insurance companies, like Sweden, Denmark and the Netherlands, tend to have far deeper capital markets than countries with smaller pools of such long-term capital (Figure 8). As discussed in our recent research (see here and here), the euro’s significant appreciation in 2025 should be generating a disinflationary impulse. If the historic pass-through elasticities hold , the peak disinflationary impact will likely occur in the first half of 2026 before gradually fading. The “second China shock” : real, but offset . FX appreciation is one reason why import prices might fall. There are other reasons, and in this regard Chinese excess capacity is worth some analysis. The ‘second China shock ’ is a tangible phenomenon. Chinese export prices to Europe have fallen sharply and now stand roughly 17% below their 2022 peak (a 30% drop in euro terms). The trend has been explicitly flagged by the ECB, referencing a term from Harvard's Kennedy School that describes China’s move up the value chain via a surge in low -priced, high-tech exports (i.e. EVs, green tech). This disinflationary push, however, is being largely neutralized. While overall Chinese export prices fell 2.5% y/y over January-November 2025, this was offset by significant price increases from other major euro area trading partners. Crucially, the combined import weight of just the US (11%), Poland (7%), and Czechia (5%) already exceeds China's (16%), and their export prices rose by +2.7%, +3.2%, and +2.5%, respectively, over the same period (Figure 1). She argues that GDP underperformance relative to the US cannot be blamed on generalized weakness in business start-ups and innovation capacity, as Europe does quite well on these metrics. Instead, it reflects a combination of societal choices such as shorter work hours and greater income redistribution, country-specific challenges such as Germany’s export dependence and France’s fiscal impasse, and a lack of “scale” in what is still largely a collection of 27 national economies. It is highly unusual for real money investors to be this overweight risk. Extreme positioning in riskier assets currently stands at +7. Looking back to Q1 2003, real money has only been this overweight— or more—for 368 days, representing just 6% of the time. On the surface, this presents a risk. If institutional investors were to become spooked, there is a significant amount of exposure that could be sold in favor of safer assets. However, history suggests this is typically not what happens. Examining positioning one month after a score of seven or higher is recorded, real money investors generally continue to maintain a risk‑on stance. Roughly half the time, positioning remains very overweight risk, while in 45% of cases exposure moderates but stays above neut ral. Although this time could prove different, historical patterns suggest that real money investors tend to hold onto their riskier positions. To quickly walk through the logic of how the seasonal factors work, we multiply a factor to the non seasonally-adjusted (NSA) index to arrive at a seasonally-adjusted (SA) version, ie: NSA = SA × SF, implying that, as a close approximation,NSAm/m ≈ SAm/m + SFm/m, and NSAm/m − SFm/m ≈ SAm/m. As a result, for a given NSA change, any change in the SF m/m feeds through to a commensurate shift in SA m/m. Moreover, they are directionally opposite; any tweak where more/less growth is explained by seasonality (SF m/m increases/ decreases) means that the other component of the NSA growth would be lower/higher, respectively. We see exactly this play out in the 2026 vintage in March, for example, where the March SF was revised lower, leading to March SF m/m decreasing, and thus March SA m/m increasing from -0.05% m/m SA to 0.03% m/m SA (Figures 3 and 4). 17 February 2026 2 Barclays | United States: Inflation Markets

The Diet at the time was in a "divided" state, where the ruling LDP-Komeito coalition held a majority in the Lower House but lacked a majority in the Upper House. The government initially nominated Toshiro Muto, then a BoJ Deputy Governor and a former Ministry of Finance (MOF) Vice Minister, for the governorship. However, the DPJ strongly opposed this, citing a violation of "the principle of separating fiscal and monetary policy." The DPJ clarified its stance against a former MOF official becoming the BoJ governor, viewing it as a threat to the central bank's independence. As a result, Muto's nomination was rejected by the Upper House. A subsequent nominee, Koji Tanami (a former MOF Vice Minister and then head of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation), was also rejected for similar reasons. Finally, the government proposed promoting Masaaki Shirakawa, who was then a deputy governor, to the position of governor, which eventually secured the DPJ's consent. Kiyohiko Nishimura, an academic economist, and Hirohide Yamaguchi, a former BoJ official, were appointed as deputy governors. G4 Central Bank Monitor The Fed, ECB, and BoJ are all approaching their neutral rates. The closer they get, the harder it is to find agreement on whether rates should move, and data dependency will be key. Our Fed cuts remain June and September despite the announcement of a new Fed Chair candidate. The timing of cuts is aligned to our outlook for inflation; we continue to expect that the Fed can execute disinflation-based rate cuts in the second half of the year. The ECB remained on hold but had a more balanced communication given a lack of acceleration in the data and EUR strength. records.text: The risks to our labor market forecast remain tilted to the downside We continue to see the risks to our labor market forecast as tilted toward a worse outcome, and we continue to see this as the key risk for the US economy in 2026. One reason is that the starting point for labor demand has not looked very healthy, at least until last week. As noted above, job growth has been weak and narrow for most of the last half year, the hiring rate has been very low, and job openings are too low and still appear to be trending lower. But the main reason that we worry about downside risk to our baseline forecast that the labor market will stabilize going forward is the possibility of a faster and more disruptive deployment of artificial intelligence (AI). While plenty of recent anecdotes point to a potentially faster rate of adoption and corresponding job losses, it is hard to know how these will translate to macroeconomic outcomes. We therefore turn to a few tools we have used to monitor and forecast the likely impact on the labor market. Exhibit 10 shows that job growth has slowed more and turned slightly negative in a handful of subindustries where AI is most ready to deploy and company-level anecdotes indicate that it is already reducing the need for workers. While the impact is visible, it remains moderate so far—we estimate that job losses in these areas have amounted to a 5-10k hit to overall job growth. Their proportion could amount to about 40%, i.e. EUR 12 bn, based on Europe’s share in global market cap of currently about 16% and assuming a certain “home bias”. Part of this amount would probably be reallocated funds from existing retail equity savings plans (both ETFs and traditional actively managed funds), which today receive on average about EUR 23 bn p.a. 15 (leaving aside a potential reallocation from old Riester contracts whose contributions hardly go into equity though). But part of it would certainly be fresh money. Assuming a 30% reallocation of the running investments (and a share of Europe of 50%), this would result in a redirection of EUR 3.5 bn currently flowing into European shares already. Bottom-line, in such a scenario, this could mean more than EUR 8 bn of additional investments in European stock markets every year. In recent years, EMs’ robust economic growth has outperformed developed markets (Exhibit 7). And while the surge in commodity prices in 2022-23 led to significant inflationary pressures, headline inflation has been broadly easing across the region and has returned to pre-Covid levels (Exhibit 8). Meanwhile, debt levels remain relatively low compared with developed markets and FX reserves have risen on average by 5pp of GDP over the past two decades (which is a significant increase in absolute terms considering how much EMs have grown in that period) (Exhibit 9 and Exhibit 10). Theoretically, these improvements in local fundamentals should provide EMs with a solid backdrop to handle shocks. 2 Hungary, which our economists’ Taylor rule estimations found to have one of the central banks that is most sensitive to FX in EM, stands as a notable exception. The FEFSA’s surplus has risen sharply in recent years as overseas interest rates have risen while the yen has weakened, reaching JPY5.4trn in FY2024. Part of the surplus is transferred annually to the next year’s general account; JPY3.2trn was transferred in FY2025, and the FY2026 draft budget calls for a JPY3.1trn transfer. Assuming an annual surplus of about JPY5trn, we estimate roughly an additional JPY2trn per year (i.e., JPY5trn−JPY3.1trn) could be transferred to the general account if the government decides to use it entirely. records.text: 16 February 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 b) Current private pension scheme (Riester) has many shortcomings In 2001, Germany introduced the so-called "Riester" pension, an additional, government-subsidised, private pension option to complement a reform of the public pension system that implied potentially declining pension levels. Although the scheme led to some uptake of private old-age provision, it fell short of its potential. Currently, there are around 15 million Riester contracts – covering only a fraction of the 37 million employees and public servants (plus spouses) who could benefit from it. The number of Riester contracts has been declining slowly since 2017 (Figure 2). Moreover, 20-25% of the contracts no longer receive contributions, according to estimates by the Federal Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (BMAS). Partly linked to that, a substantial share – about 6 million Riester contracts – do not receive public subsidies. A silver lining is that Germans are increasingly aware of this and many are willing to take on more responsibility for their retirement planning. Thus, a well-designed “old-age provision account” could help to channel more retail savings from low-interest bank deposits and insurance claims into higher-yielding stock markets at low cost. Indeed, in the long run, this has the potential to become a true game-changer for German households’ financial well-being in their old age. Beyond the individual benefits, a stronger funded pension pillar could have positive knock-on effects on the broader economy. It would pool long-term capital that is well positioned to finance innovative, high-growth companies as well as infrastructure investments. This is especially true for humanoids, where their many degrees of freedom push actuator-related costs to roughly half of the total bill of materials. As physical AI adoption accelerates, demand for high-precision actuators will continue to rise. As a result, actuators could emerge as a critical bottleneck in robot production, increasing the importance of a reliable supply chain. In our view, Europe's deeply rooted expertise in precision mechanics—honed through decades of industrial engineering, from automotive to advanced manufacturing—will position the region well to meet this demand. Our analysis of UN Comtrade, the world's most comprehensive trade database, shows Europe (EEA + Switzerland) is already the leading supplier of actuator systems and actuator parts. Europe accounts for 34% of global actuator-related supply (Figure 15), ahead of China (26%), Mexico (9%), Japan (5%) and the US (5%). Germany alone accounts for about one-third of Europe's actuator supply. Thus, as physical AI robotics expand, actuators could support Europe in securing a strategic advantage. Against this backdrop, Tesla offers a clear case study. The company opened its 4Q earnings call by announcing that it would end production of Models S/X by next quarter, with autonomy (Robotaxi, FSD) and humanoid robots becoming Tesla's core growth priorities in the years ahead. On the surface, the operational effect is limited; these models have had marginal relevance for quite some time, accounting for just 2% of Tesla's volume in 2025. Thus, we think the significance of this move is largely symbolic for now: a passing of the baton from Auto to AI, and more specifically into physical AI. However, it will likely push capex higher in 2026 and keep it elevated for years as Tesla invests heavily in technology and chip capacity. Unlocking automation potential in warehousing, logistics and manufacturing This shift toward physical AI is already evident in large-scale logistics and retail operations. Companies with complex supply chains such as Amazon and Walmart, already illustrate how automation and robotics can improve efficiency and safety by taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks. records.text: tal content such as text, images and code, physical AI is defined by its ability to close the loop between perception, decision and real-world action. Physical AI is the toughest frontier in AI because these systems must master physics, causality and time to truly work in the real world. In practice, this evolution transforms AI from a tool for efficiency and knowledge synthesis into an active agent of physical work within the real economy, enabling machines to execute complex tasks in dynamic, real-world settings. Physical AI is also referred to as embodied AI; in this report, for brevity, we use the terms robot and physical AI interchangeably, assuming a robot to be an AI-enabled physical machine. Our definition of physical AI includes four main technologies,1 each covering a range of autonomy from assisted to fully autonomous operation: • Humanoid robots: Robots designed to behave and look like humans, built for human- centred environments and tasks. For an in-depth analysis of humanoid robotics and its implications for productivity, labour markets and the future of work, please refer to our report The future of work: AI gets physical (14 January 2026). • Autonomous vehicles and mobility: Self-driving vehicles and systems that move people or goods on their own, ranging from assisted-driving cars and self-driving trucks to full robotaxis. • Advanced industrial automation: AI-enabled robots performing physical tasks in factories and logistics, including collaborative robots

records.text: 16 February 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG 1) Why Germany needs a strong funded pension pillar a) Pay-as-you-go system reaches its limits in an aging society Germany’s pension system is predominantly built on the pay-as-you-go statutory pension insurance. Demographic change, with an aging society, lower birth rates, and a probably shrinking population going forward, 1 is putting strains on the system. In 2024, the birth rate dropped to only 1.35 children per woman, on average, which is the lowest figure in nearly 20 years. In the coming years, the “baby boomers” will retire, with the number of people above statutory retirement age likely to grow from currently around 17.6 million (20% of total population) to 20 million by 2035 (24%). By 2040, for each retiree there will be only two contributors to the statutory pension, i.e. people of working age, down from currently 2½ (with immigration unlikely to change the picture substantially). 2 Already today, the statutory pension insurance requires a staggering additional funding of EUR 128 bn from the federal budget for 2026 (24% of the core budget). Overall, there is considerable fiscal consolidation pressure, which may lead to a lower pension level in the future.3 It is therefore paramount that Germans can also rely on a strong funded pension to secure their standard of living in old age. We incorporate our equity analysts' outlook for higher hyperscaler capex, and raise our growth forecasts for the US higher by 20bp, to 2.6% in 2026. Revisions to payrolls point to faster growth in productivity – data show elements of a demand-driven and supply-driven boost to the economy, and which one wins will determine the path for inflation and unemployment. The recent Japan election brought a majority government for Takaichi - we view fiscal concerns as overdone and believe the political mandate could help extend the Japan reflation story. The Year of Risk Reboot: Despite headlines around policy uncertainty, micro and macro fundamentals are solid. Resilient growth – powered by capex, AI efficiency gains, and easing – can boost earnings and lower default rates, favouring stocks and HY credit. For US and Japan in particular, fiscal and deregulation serve as additional tailwinds. And while the debate about the "end of US exceptionalism" has returned, flows don’t point to a paradigm shift yet, and TINA still rules for US markets. Zooming in further to the behaviour of EM HY local rates around these risk-off episodes suggests a remarkable convergence between EM and DM rates, and strengthens the results on resilience in two distinct ways. First, widening the window of study to 8 days (as opposed to 1) after the global risk-off shock suggests that not only is the post-shock selloff in EM rates more muted, but that by the end of the week the move lower in rates across EM low- and high-yielders is more or less similar in magnitude to that in G10 rates. In other words, EM rates are increasingly acting to ease local financial conditions in response to global shocks, similar to DM rates, even if it takes a few days to get there in the case of the high-yielders. Second, this shift in behaviour is not simply an artefact of where the sample has been separated. That said, since pay growth is largely target-consistent, it is not immediately clear further sharp deceleration is warranted to ensure inflation falls and remains at the 2% target. BoE implications: Indeed, as the majority of the MPC - or rather, the crucial Bailey/ Breeden/Ramsden nexus - starts to feel more comfortable in prioritising the real economy amid ongoing disinflation, more rate cuts are likely. With the BoE forecasting the jobless rate at 5.1% for 4Q, today's print bodes well for a cut in March, with risks of follow-up action as early as June vs. our current base case of July. The important part of the puzzle, however, is disinflation - the MPC will want to see some progress in disinflation at the start of the year. Hence, tomorrow's inflation print remains the key data release ahead of March. At 3% headline and core inflation, our forecast, we think, is aligned with the move in March, and guidance that ultimately allows for some further easing.

Blended approach more likely: Instead, we expect the NT to affirm its commitment to pursuing a debt-stabilising primary balance target through continued pursuit of ‘soft’ expenditure ceilings. Added to this framework is likely to be the more qualitative aspects of a fiscal anchor. These, we believe, will centre around a clearer set of principles and standards around which a ‘sustainable’ budget is set. The NT’s fiscal anchor discussion document references a desire to cement a defined set of “procedures, processes and reporting requirements” for all government departments to meet each year ahead of the passing of the national budget policy statement every February. Arguably, the NT has already begun to embed this principles-led approach, in response to last year’s two failed attempts to pass its national budget. The absence of a strict, rules-based anchor could perhaps come as a disappointment to a market which continues to display a solid degree of exuberance towards SAGBs. That said, we think any move to formalise a commitment to fiscal consolidation and lock in short-term cyclical tailwinds to the NT’s already growing primary surplus forecasts is likely to be welcomed. This helps us assess whether these shifts relate to the recent uptick in European M&A and what they may signal for the forward-looking pipeline. The results are shown in Exhibit 4 (non-Financials on the left, Financials on the right). The most notable shift over the past 1-2 years is the fading of macroeconomic headwinds. Mentions of ‘inflation’, ‘interest rates’ and ‘economic slowdown’ have declined across both groups. For non-financial firms, that improvement has been partly offset by more references to China and competitive pressures, and tariffs. For financial firms, the focus has tilted toward innovation and digital transformation, alongside a modest rise in government policy mentions and finally tariffs. Overall, this pattern suggests that part of the rebound in European M&A is cyclical, as easing macro headwinds have supported stronger growth in recent years. Even so, current transcripts do not sound overly optimistic, with limited discussion of tailwinds, language you might otherwise expect to precede a debt-funded M&A boom. We would caveat that this type of keyword screen is highly sensitive to the specific terms used and, on its own, is not a reliable indicator of the future direction of European M&A. Today's actuator systems consume substantial power and can empty batteries rapidly, especially under heavy or continuous motion. Adding more batteries does not help lightweight robots, since the extra mass becomes counterproductive. Because of this, current battery technology translates into short run times. Drone flight times often remain under 30 minutes. Humanoid robots can typically operate for 4-5 hours, falling to 2-4 hours during heavy motion.12 Run times could improve with better storage technologies (such as silicon-based batteries) and reductions in energy demand through more efficient actuators, fewer joints, lower system weight and more efficient battery-swap mechanisms. Exhibit 6 reveals several key observations: First, EM and G9 currencies (with the exception of JPY and CHF) typically depreciate against the USD during risk-off periods. Second, while G10 and EM low-yielder front-end rates tend to rally, high-yielders have historically sold off. However, a clear shift has occurred in the past five years regarding the FX and rate dynamics of high-yielders. While their currencies have continued to weaken by approximately the same magnitude in response to shocks, their front-end rates have now begun to rally during risk-off events.2 This suggests that, on balance, the market now perceives EM central banks as being under less pressure to hike rates in response to global shocks. In part, that is likely to be about institutional improvements – the IMF study suggests that better macro resilience to risk-off shocks can be attributed to improvements in monetary policy frameworks. To the extent that this holds at the macro level, it should also apply in explaining the resilience of EM assets (particularly rates) around global risk-offs, as the markets serve as the initial point of contact for the transmission of global shocks to the broader economy. At the heart of this system are actuators, which combine electric motors, gears and other components to generate motion in each joint. These drive the overall movement, while supporting elements like wheels, casings and wiring help the robot stay functional. Together, they form the physical force behind what the robot's brain instructs it to do. Actuators' power, made in Europe Actuators enable a wide range of movements required across physical AI applications. They drive drone propellers, humanoid hands, autonomous vehicle steering mechanisms, and robotic arms in manufacturing, among many other applications (Figure 14). Because nearly all electrically driven movement depends on precise, compact actuators, they form the essential mechanical foundation of physical AI. FIGURE 14. Actuators enable a broad spectrum of movements across physical AI Source: Barclays Research Recent advances in actuator technology have improved robot precision, response speed and torque control, boosting dexterity and making robots safer to deploy. Physical AI: The next trillion dollar market? Physical AI marks a fundamental paradigm shift from AI confined to digital spaces to intelligent systems that sense, think and act in the real word. By comparing the resulting "core" proxies from the 2026 versus 2025 seasonal vintages from the BLS, we get slightly different paths, although for most high-level purposes, the trend is largely similar, holding between 15-20bp for most of the rest of 2026 (Figure 9). One thing specifically to note: in our methodology, we model energy commodities NSA, convert to energy commodities SA using the latest BLS seasonal factor, and then strip the result out of headline SA to get ex-energy commodities SA (which we use as a proxy for the core path). This structure is inherently sensitive to both the headline and energy commodities seasonal vectors, and because the October energy commodities seasonal factor specifically was changed meaningfully, this passes through to a noisier "core" fixings path in H2 26 (Figure 10). That said, we may still be early for how the market digests this information. A look at fixings trades posted to SDR on Friday following the January CPI release shows a total of one trade (targeting the February 2026 CPI NSA print), and that was only listed late afternoon. 17 February 2026 5 Barclays | United States: Inflation Markets

We expect broad political backing for infrastructure-led spending priorities; spending reviews of inefficient state programmes; formalisation of a fiscal anchor framework; and little-to-no debate on tax rises yet. KEY MESSAGES South Africa’s 2026 national budget should firmly align with November’s mid-term consolidation strategy. We forecast a main budget deficit for FY2025/26 at 0.3pp of GDP less than Treasury forecasts, as buoyant tax revenues continue to meet spending restraints. Room for corporate revenue upgrades, thanks to commodity price windfalls, is unlikely to be fully incorporated. We see further upside risk to primary surplus estimates and another reduction in issuance in the Q4 2026 mid-term budget. Better fiscal starting points mean that the NT is on track to stabilise debt ratios below 78% of GDP in FY2026/27. We expect the NT to give more colour on the formalisation of a fiscal anchor but stop short of a rigid rule-based approach to debt stabilisation. Confirmation that South Africa’s fiscal position is at a positive inflection point should keep supporting a flatter curve and room for credit rating upgrades in 2026/27. In all models considered here, supplementary pension products are usually distributed by private providers like banks, investment funds and insurance companies. They are under close supervision by financial regulators, adding an additional layer of assurance over private pension savings. Flexibility and security in the payout phase can also contribute to the attractiveness of retirement savings models. n Providing a steady additional income in retirement. Most models encourage the disbursement of accumulated private old-age provision funds in the form of an annuity rather than lump-sum payouts. This is also the case in Germany with a choice between two payout modes (lifelong or fixed-duration annuity). In models without guarantees, 20% of the capital can remain invested and thus potentially generate further returns. In Sweden, the UK (“flexi-access”) and many US IRAs, the accumulated capital also remains invested during the payout phase. n Limited early withdrawals. As the savings are intended to be used in old age, most schemes limit early withdrawals. While the UK and Estonia have exceptions only for health reasons, in France, Poland and the US, funds can also be withdrawn early to buy a home. In Germany, early withdrawals for energy-efficient renovations or barrier-free living in owner-occupied homes remain possible, with simplified rules. n Ensuring survivor’s benefits.

records.text: 6 Insights Information Classification: General Appendix Note on Percentiles We use percentiles to gauge the significance of a flow or positioning metric over a variety of time periods and countries. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. A reading in the 50th percentile would signal that net flows in the asset over the period are at zero. We use a simple colour coding scheme to highlight strong (top 20 th percentile) and weak (bottom 20th percentile) flows. We percentile our FX Holdings indicators in the same, conditional fashion, using the same five-year look-back period, as FX flows. This should feed into healthy corporate income tax revenues later this year. Amazon has over 1mn robots operating in its fulfilment network, which is likely still only a fraction of the long-term potential. Amazon has highlighted a suite of task-specific systems: Sequoia, which brings inventory to employee workstations to improve ergonomics; Proteus, which moves order carts alongside workers; and Vulcan, which navigates cluttered spaces using sight and touch. records.text: M Update Japan Economics | Japan US Investor Visit: Post Ruling Party Landslide in Lower House Election Morgan Stanley MUFG Securities Co., Ltd. Masayuki Inui Economist Masayuki.Inui@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-5407 Takeshi Yamaguchi Chief Japan Economist Takeshi.Yamaguchi@morganstanleymufg.com +81 3 6836-5404 Visit to US investors after ruling party landslide: In the week of Feb 9, right after Japan’s Lower House election, Masayuki Inui from the Japan Economics team visited US investors. Numerous meetings were held with equity and fixed income investors, including senior participants such as fund CIOs, CEOs, and founders. Joint roundtable discussions were also hosted with the US economics and rates teams. Overall, the visit was very well attended and highly constructive. Our betas suggest that for a 1% increase in FX reserves (as a % of GDP), rates respond on average by moving 0.1bp lower during risk-offs. On the other hand, markets with higher levels of external debt are likely to respond more adversely during global risk-offs, consistent with an increased risk of capital outflows. On average, our estimates suggest that for a 1% increase in external debt (as a % of GDP), rates respond with a 0.15bp move higher during global risk-offs. Second, while less statistically significant, our results also suggest that when inflation remains unanchored relative to central banks’ targets, rates respond more adversely to risk-off shocks. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

This is the direct cause of the staggered term-end dates for the governor and deputy governors that persist to this day. The 2012 policy board member appointment: a conflict over the monetary easing stance In April 2012, the DPJ administration under Prime Minister Yoshihiko Noda nominated the private-sector economist Ryutaro Kono to succeed policy board member Seiji Nakamura, whose term was expiring. However, the nomination was rejected by the Upper House, where the ruling party lacked a majority at the time. The main reason for the opposition from the LDP, then an opposition party, was that Kono was perceived as being cautious about aggressive monetary easing. At that time, escaping deflation was recognized as an urgent task for the Japanese economy, and the LDP was demanding more drastic monetary easing from the BoJ. Kono's appointment was judged to be inconsistent with this policy direction. Is this time different? More specifically, will AI prove to be more of a substitute for than a complement to the labour market and result in lower, rather than higher, expected wages, thereby depressing demand? There is a plausible argument that the scale of AI and its speed of adoption increase the odds that it will be a substitute for labour, at least in the short term. Moreover, the labour market will most likely lag financial markets if there are risks of a significant disruption. This tempers the comfort one takes from resilient data. There are valid counterarguments, such as “speed bumps” in the adoption of AI due, for instance, to regulation, accountability or validation processes. However, irrespective of the right answer, the uncertainty by itself may be enough to dampen demand in the short term. Longer term, however, one should be sceptical of statements that technological progress will result in structurally low inflation. Technological progress primarily changes relative prices. General inflation will, as always in a world of fiat money, be determined by the fiscal and monetary policy mix. records.text: 16 February 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 3) What is the government’s plan for private pension reform? The government aims to make private pension provision more attractive, allowing for a broader product range that is at the same time more transparent than the old system and offers cheaper and return-oriented solutions. This could pave the way for a stronger stock market orientation within the third pillar. Key elements of the draft law adopted by the cabinet on December 17 are: Introduction of a return-oriented “old-age provision account” (“Altersvorsorgedepot”). Contributions will be invested in actively or passively managed investment funds (up to a risk class of 5), with the investor carrying the risk. As an alternative option for risk-averse investors, guarantee products that secure 100% or 80% of the contributions continue to be available. An upper limit at risk class 5 means that e.g. a broad and well-diversified Dax ETF is generally considered the highest possible risk still accepted under the new framework (even though the Dax moved from class 5 to class 4 a few months ago). However, this could lead to a lower acceptance rate of such stock ETFs, given that people tend to avoid the extremes or “corner solutions” in a certain distribution if they can choose freely. Emerging vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual inputs, language understanding, and action outputs, helping connect perception and behaviour as part of the learning process. However, adoption remains in the early stages. Training complexities run across physical AI technologies. Take autonomous vehicles as an example. These AI models do not just learn traffic signs and road rules; they also need to understand how objects around them move, how they themselves move under physics principles (gravity, inertia), how to react instantly to unexpected events, like a pedestrian falling nearby, and how to handle messy real-world conditions like rain, traffic jams or unpredictable human behaviour. Similar complexities arise when training humanoid robots, as they must first learn to continuously maintain balance while moving, avoiding falls and collisions, and then crucially learn to handle diverse objects with dexterity. Collecting and training physical-world data is slow, costly and potentially risky for the public. As a result, physical AI models lean heavily on simulators that recreate the real world. These platforms run 'digital twins' of factories, warehouses or even entire cities, essentially video games for robots. records.text: Walmart is following a similar trajectory. Its next-generation, more automated fulfilment centres are already twice as productive as legacy facilities, with further gains to come as robotics are integrated into additional processes. Current deployments focus on strenuous activities such as lifting products on and off pallets, while AI-assisted pallet tracking helps reduce damage in fresh and fragile categories. AI-enabled robotic systems are also improving pickup and delivery speeds at stores, reinforcing Walmart's broader strategy to modernise its supply chain through automation. The next wave of industrial automation: Humanoids The experiences of Amazon and Walmart show how quickly robotics are reshaping supply chains, while also highlighting where systems designed to perform specific tasks may eventually reach their limits. As automation capabilities broaden, humanoid robots are emerging as a natural next step, offering more flexibility in environments built for people. With labour dynamics becoming more pronounced due to population ageing, the potential use cases for humanoid systems are beginning to crystallise. Following their substantial correction, Chinese export prices have reconverged with the domestic Producer Price Index (Figure 5). We view PPI as a crucial anchor for export prices because it represents the factory -gate cost of production. While exporting firms can temporarily sell below this cost to capture market share – the essence of "involution" – they cannot do so indefinitely without incurring un sustainable losses. Therefore, in the medium term, PPI should act like a gravitational floor for export prices. Challenges in Triggering Snap Elections: It is important to remember that the process leading to early elections is more complex than in many other jurisdictions. Only the President of the Republic has the authority to dissolve Parliament, and the departure of a single party from the majority does not automatically necessitate snap elections. Instead, a new government could potentially be formed by a different coalition capable of securing a parliamentary majority. For instance, in the summer of 2019, Mr. Salvini withdrew from the Five Star Movement/League government with the intention of triggering snap elections, counting on his party's then-high popularity, which could have led to his appointment as Prime Minister. However, a new coalition government comprising the Democratic Party (PD) and the Five Star Movement was subsequently formed without recourse to new elections. 3. records.text: Sara Grut +44(20)7774-8622 | sara.grut@gs.com Goldman Sachs International Global Markets Daily: European M&A: Sentiment Improves, Debt-Funded Deal Boom Unlikely 17 February 2026 | 10:50AM GMT Strategic M&A volumes in Europe reached $257 billion last year, near the upper n end of the historical range but still well below the roughly $1.4 trillion recorded in the US. The gap is equally visible in credit markets, where M&A-related issuance in the EUR IG market totaled just €7 billion last year vs. $146 billion in USD IG. In this Global Markets Daily, we discuss why this divergence is likely to persist and n what signals from recent firm transcripts imply for the European M&A pipeline. We think a meaningful portion of the gap is structural, as US deal flow is more skewed toward Tech and mega-cap transactions, an ecosystem that remains far smaller in Europe. Firm transcripts suggest M&A is being discussed more among EUR IG issuers, n especially Financials, alongside fewer mentions of macroeconomic headwinds. Among non-Financials, macroeconomic concerns appear to be fading but are giving way to concerns around competition from China and tariffs. Overall, we think the recent rise in European M&A looks cyclical, while a sustained step-change likely requires structural reforms. Hence, we think M&A-driven supply risk remains skewed toward the USD market. records.text: FOCUS F O C U S 16/02/2026 1 Japan: Consumption tax cut plan – fiscal food for thought The prime minister’s commitment: The central focus of fiscal policy in Japan in the near term is linked inextricably to the fate of the planned consumption-tax cut, we argue. Ahead of the recent lower-house election, the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which had previously adopted a cautious stance on a consumption tax cut, shifted its position dramatically under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. The party pledged to accelerate the debate on a two-year, zero-rate food-tax cut, and won a landslide victory. Since the election the prime minister has reiterated her intention to pursue the tax cut without issuing “deficit- financing bonds”, stating that details of the financing and timetable will be debated in the forthcoming National Council, with an interim report of the plan to be compiled by the summer. Prior to the election, market participants were skeptical about the feasibility of the tax cut. Nevertheless, we have consistently argued that the cut is likely to materialize, and the election result has only reinforced that view. Although some fiscally-conservative LDP members remain wary, the prime minister’s decisive electoral mandate strengthens her influence within the party. Personal pension provision is typically voluntary, and Germany plans to keep it optional. This can result in limited uptake, mainly attracting participants with higher income. An exception is the mandatory premium pension in Sweden to which every person with a “pensionable income” 19 must contribute. The Swedish premium pension thus covers 80% of the population (incl. both active savers and also pensioners), which is a far higher share than in most voluntary systems. However, these too can reach many people, as in Switzerland. Here, 78% of the population has a private pension account,20 albeit often without an equity component. 21 This shows that well- designed voluntary schemes can achieve broad coverage. Auto-enrolment could offer a possible middle ground, as recently recommended by the European Commission. This is envisaged for the proposed “early start pension” in Germany, where a pension savings account would automatically be opened for all children from the age of six. Automatic enrolment worked well for voluntary occupational pension schemes in New Zealand (“KiwiSaver”) and the UK (workplace pensions), with participation rates of 86% and 52% of working-age 19 This includes salaries, but also parental allowance, unemployment benefits, sickness compensation, or taxable income from business operations. 20 Raiffeisen and ZHAW (2025). We think the prime minister may well have had such an idea in mind when she made a remark to the effect during the election campaign that a weak yen is benefiting the FEFSA. Bear in mind, however, that the FEFSA’s assets are mostly denominated in foreign currency, and the government will not be selling foreign assets to generate yen cash because that could be interpreted as FX intervention. In accounting terms, a transfer of the FEFSA’s surplus to the general account allows the government to reduce “deficit-financing bonds” booked in its general account; in practice, it will not necessarily reduce the government’s overall borrowing needs. Part of the transfer might be funded by yen cash that the FEFSA holds, but it would likely be funded largely by issuing financing bills (booked in the FEFSA). We would also note that even if the transfer were to be funded partly by the yen cash that the FEFSA holds, the government’s net financial debt would increase as its assets decrease. Similarly, even if the government were to liquidate its foreign assets to pay for the tax cut, the government’s net financial debt would also increase. In any case, we think the portion financed by cutting expenditure or raising other taxes would likely be modest, and net fiscal expansion resulting from the consumption tax cut would likely be meaningful, although it would be somewhat smaller than 0.8% of GDP. EM assets have enjoyed a strong start in 2026 after a year of stellar returns in n 2025. But the volatility in markets, wrought by tech stock wobbles, drawdowns in precious metals, and geopolitical risks, have raised concerns that EM assets could be vulnerable to these external shocks, even if domestic macro fundamentals are sound. The concern is understandable, but in our assessment investor perception of the n riskiness of EM assets now lags the reality. We show that EM assets are demonstrating more resilience over time, and over the past five years – a period rich in global shocks – the response of EM assets to global risk-off episodes indicates a shift from historical patterns and is more akin to the behaviour of many DM assets. That increased resilience is particularly striking in the case of EM local rates (and n especially high-yielder local rates). EM rates are increasingly acting to ease local financial conditions in response to global shocks, similar to DM rates, even if it takes a few days to get there. In effect, EM central banks are now perceived as facing less pressure to tighten policy during global risk-offs, allowing local monetary policy to respond to local growth/inflation dynamics. Several factors suggest the most intense phase of Chinese price deflation is passing. First, the share of exports from China with sharp price cuts is not unprecedented and has eased from its early 2025 peak. Second, and more fundamentally, a cost -based floor may be forming as export prices have reconverged with domestic PPI, which itself has now started to rise month-on-month. Third, this bottoming out process is consistent with Beijing's anti-"involution" policy gaining traction, limiting the scope for further deep and sustained price drops. Our China economists expect PPI to rise in H2, suggesting further disinflationary pressure on the euro area may be contained to H1. • Real risk shifting from prices to activity. Inflation-driven revenue growth: Tax revenues have undoubtedly been growing robustly in Japan in recent years due largely to inflation. Japan’s fiscal framework has few mechanisms that automatically adjust either revenues or expenditures in response to inflation; as inflation rises, revenues are boosted by bracket creep, while regular spending tends to be suppressed in real terms. Partly thanks to this, the primary-balance deficit for the national and local governments fell to 1.8 % of GDP in FY2024 and is projected by the Cabinet Office at 1.3% of GDP for FY2025, despite having repeatedly resorted to discretionary stimulus measures. Against this backdrop, the administration will likely argue that the benefit-linked tax credit will be financed in part by “natural” tax-revenue gains and will not rely on “deficit-financing bonds,” as was the case with the consumption-tax cut. At any rate, we expect the government to pursue a more expansionary fiscal stance under Prime Minister Takaichi, while taking some account of financial markets’ potential reaction. As the economy is near full employment, we expect fiscal expansion to maintain upward pressure on the underlying inflation trend.
